content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations regarding the use of home-based records for maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH). These records are intended to complement facility-based records and are kept at home by individuals or caregivers, either in paper or electronic format. They document the history of health services received by an individual. Home-based records can range from antenatal notes or vaccination-only cards to more comprehensive maternal and child health books, which often include health education messages. These records are used in at least 163 countries, though their design and content vary significantly. In some countries, nearly everyone retains a home-based record, while in others, usage is lower. Despite their widespread implementation over decades, the benefits of home-based records had not been systematically reviewed until recently. WHO has now published a guideline providing updated, evidence-based recommendations on their use to improve MNCH outcomes. The guideline was developed using WHO’s standard process for guideline development, overseen by a WHO Steering Group. Systematic reviews of both quantitative and qualitative evidence were conducted, along with a framework analysis of grey literature and key informant interviews. The quality, certainty, and confidence of the evidence were assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) and CERQual (Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research) approaches. Meetings of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), an international group of experts, were held in November 2017 and April 2018 to review the evidence and develop recommendations. The GDG evaluated evidence based on criteria such as impact, potential harms, stakeholder value, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The final guideline was published in September 2018. Recommendations: 1. The use of home-based records, as a complement to facility-based records, is recommended for the care of pregnant women, mothers, newborns, and children. These records can improve care-seeking behaviors, male involvement and support within households, maternal and child home care practices, infant and child feeding, and communication between health providers and women/caregivers. However, the evidence supporting these benefits is of low certainty. 2. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether any specific type, format, or design of home-based records is more effective. Policymakers should engage stakeholders to discuss considerations regarding the type, content, and implementation of home-based records. Observations from the GDG: Some studies demonstrated positive effects on maternal health, immunization, care-seeking behaviors, supportive home environments for MNCH care, infant feeding, child growth and development, continuity of care, and communication with healthcare providers. Qualitative evidence indicates that women, caregivers, and providers across various settings value home-based records. Limitations of the evidence include a small number of studies, many of which were conducted in high-income countries or are outdated (pre-2000). Additionally, for many outcomes, no significant effects were reported, or no studies were available. Implementation Considerations: The effectiveness of home-based records in improving MNCH outcomes depends on the quality of their implementation. Key considerations include: Design and Content: Records should avoid including personal information that could lead to stigma or discrimination (e.g., HIV status). They should be adapted to local contexts, considering health priorities, available services, and language. In settings with low literacy, records should include more images and less text. For countries with multipurpose records, content should be harmonized to promote continuity of care. Training: Health workers require initial and refresher training, as well as supervision, to ensure records are completed correctly. They should also remind individuals and caregivers to retain and bring their records to every facility visit. Planning: Strong government ownership and leadership are essential for prioritizing and sustaining home-based records. Regular redesigns are necessary to keep health information up to date, with timelines set to avoid delays and stock-outs. Continuous supply and availability of updated records should be ensured through existing health system supply chains. Health Education: Home-based records alone may not be sufficient to improve care practices and care-seeking behaviors. Comprehensive health promotion and communication strategies are needed, with home-based records serving as one component. Research Gaps: More robust evidence is needed to determine the best ways to implement home-based records to ensure their impact on MNCH and health service outcomes. Key areas for further research include: Consensus on key implementation components and outcome measurements for evaluating home-based records. Benefits of using home-based records for single versus multiple aspects of health, and their role in health education. Longitudinal studies and household surveys to monitor and improve implementation. Linking home-based records to formal health information systems and assessing the impact. Effects of home-based records on equity across subpopulations. Impact on early child development outcomes. User-friendly designs for effective home-based records. Whether home-based records should be distributed for free. Use of incentive schemes (financial and non-financial) to encourage appropriate use of home-based records. Funding for the development of the guideline and related products was provided by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).
